subject: Is there a better way to code this zero-inflated model?

messages.author: 747a39cfe1be5cdb
messages.subject: Is there a better way to code this zero-inflated model?
parts:
I'm working with a zero-inflated Poisson regression model with Gaussian fixed and random effects, and I'm surprised that the posterior distribution of some of the random effects is skewed. I've attached the model I'm using as a .stan file. I think there are a lot of things in the model that I could be coding much better. Does anyone on the list have any advice on improvements that I could make?

Mark

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is there a better way to code this zero-inflated model?
parts:
The coding will affect efficiency, but not the posterior.

Why is it surprising the random effects are skewed (I don't have
much experience here).

For coding tips, the biggest one is to follow the multivariate
normal example for random effects in the regression chapter of the manual.
We finally wrote up our recommended practices for efficiency and priors.
Inverse Wishart isn't your friend --- it's only standard practice in
BUGS/JAGs because they can only handle conjugate multivariate distributions.

You also want to vectorize wherever possible. So

for (m in 1:M)
vu[m] ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);

should be:

v ~ multi_normal(zeros_u, sigma_u);

I'd also stay away from beta(0.01,0.01) priors unless you have some
reason for wanting to push the posterior toward the boundaries.

for (i in 1:P)
zeros_beta[i] <- 0.0;

can be reduced to

zeros_beta <- rep_vector(0, P);

I don't have the patience to work it out, but if you could replace

for (n in 1:N) {
for (m in 1:M)
for (b in 1:B)
u[(m-1)*B+b] <- vu[m][b];


with matrix operations, it'd most likely be faster.

Replace

poisson_log(y[n], exp(eta))

with poisson_log_log(y[n], eta);

poisson_log() takes its parameter on the log scale, and poisson_log_log is
the function.

- Bob
